title: Review: Experimental design and variables; Nucleotides, DNA and RNA structure; Translation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM10a#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t1 term and clue written for the game; PR01b#t2 term and clue written for the game; GE05a#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM10a#N.9, BM10b#N.15, GE05a#N.4, PR01b#N.12, BM10a#N.12a, BM10b#N.6a, GE05a#N.10, PR01b#N.5, BM10a#N.2a, GE05a#N.7, BM10a#N.8, BM10a#N.11a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Nucleotide
items.clue: Monomer of DNA and RNA: a pentose, a phosphate and a base

items.label: Random error
items.clue: Unpredictable scatter in readings; repeats and a mean reduce its effect.

items.label: Systematic error
items.clue: Shifts every reading the same way; removed by calibrating, not by repeats.

items.label: Translation
items.clue: Using the base sequence of mRNA to build the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide.

questions.stem: Analysis of a sample of double-stranded DNA from a hypothetical bacterium shows that 21% of its nitrogenous bases are adenine. What percentage of its bases are cytosine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, so T = A = 21% and A + T = 42%. That leaves 100% − 42% = 58% for C and G together, and because C = G, cytosine is 58%/2 = 29%.

questions.stem: Two DNA molecules from two hypothetical species of bacteria each contain the same number of nucleotides, and in both, 30% of the bases are adenine, 30% thymine, 20% guanine and 20% cytosine. The two molecules carry different genetic information. Which statement best explains how this is possible?

options.text: The amino acids attached along their strands are arranged in a different order in each.
The nucleotides of each species are built around a different five-carbon sugar.
Each molecule is folded into a different three-dimensional shape that stores information.
Their nucleotides are arranged in a different order along each molecule.

questions.stem: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?

options.text: It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.

questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.stem: A student uses a water bath to keep enzyme tubes at 30 °C. Her thermometer gives readings that agree closely: 30.0, 30.0, 30.5, 30.0 °C. A calibrated electronic probe in the same water bath reads 28.0 °C. Which improvement would make her temperature measurements more accurate?

options.text: Take ten readings with the same thermometer and use their mean.
Calibrate the thermometer against the probe, or use the probe instead.
Record each reading to two decimal places, so that the mean is more exact.
Calculate the range of her readings, to show that they are accurate.

questions.explanation: The readings are precise but about 2 °C high: a systematic error. Only calibration (or a calibrated instrument) brings the readings close to the true value.

questions.stem: A solution of DNA is heated to 95 °C. The two strands separate, but each strand remains a continuous, intact chain of nucleotides. Which explanation is consistent with these observations?

options.text: The backbone of each strand is covalently bonded, so it survives heating that breaks the weaker hydrogen bonds between the strands.
The hydrogen bonds of the backbone are stronger than the covalent bonds between strands, so only the strands come apart.
Heating breaks the covalent bonds that join the two strands, while the hydrogen bonds within each strand stay intact.
The bases along each strand are covalently bonded to one another, which holds the strand together when the pairs separate.

questions.stem: The template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGGA at one position. What base sequence will the mRNA transcribed from it have at that position?

options.text: AUGCCU
UACGGA
ATGCCT
CGUAAG

questions.explanation: RNA nucleotides are added by complementary base pairing with the template: A pairs with U, T with A, C with G and G with C. So TACGGA gives AUGCCU.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the first nucleotide of the start codon to the last nucleotide of the stop codon, is 903 nucleotides long. How many amino acids does the polypeptide translated from this region contain?
questions.explanation: 903 ÷ 3 = 301 codons. AUG codes for methionine and the stop codon codes for nothing, so the polypeptide has 301 − 1 = 300 amino acids.

questions.stem: A potato cylinder's mass falls from 3.62 g to 3.40 g in a sucrose solution. The balance reads to ±0.01 g. What is the percentage error in the change in mass?
questions.explanation: Change = 3.62 − 3.40 = 0.22 g, uncertainty = 0.01 + 0.01 = ±0.02 g (OCR form: 2 × 0.01). Percentage error = 0.02 ÷ 0.22 × 100 = 9.1%. A small change carries a large percentage error.

questions.stem: Which is a correct description of a single nucleotide?

options.text: A nitrogenous base only; the sugar and phosphate belong to the backbone.
A pentose sugar bonded to a phosphate group and to a nitrogenous base.
A phosphate group bonded to a nitrogenous base, which is bonded to a sugar.
A six-carbon sugar, glucose, bonded to a phosphate and to a base.

questions.explanation: A nucleotide has three components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The sugar is central, with the phosphate and the base each bonded to it.

questions.stem: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?

options.text: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how the two strands of a DNA double helix are held together?

options.text: By hydrogen bonds between identical bases, such as A with A, one on each strand
By covalent bonds between complementary bases, with one base on each strand
By hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one base on each strand
By covalent bonds joining the sugar–phosphate backbones of the two strands

questions.explanation: The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, one from each strand: adenine pairs with thymine and cytosine with guanine. The nucleotides within each strand are joined by covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Which row correctly gives differences between DNA and RNA?

options.text: DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: two strands, ribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, thymine.
DNA: two strands, ribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, deoxyribose, uracil.
DNA: two strands, deoxyribose, thymine. RNA: one strand, ribose and uracil.

questions.explanation: DNA is double-stranded, contains the pentose deoxyribose and has thymine; RNA is single-stranded, contains ribose and has uracil in place of thymine.
